Trinidad & Tobago

Beryl McBurnie

Beryl Eugenia McBurnie, affectionately and respectfully known as the "First Lady of Dance" in Trinidad and Tobago, was a pioneering dancer, choreographer, and cultural visionary. At a time when European classical arts were positioned as the only legitimate forms of cultural expression in the colonial Caribbean, McBurnie dedicated her life to unearthing, celebrating, and institutionalizing the rich, vibrant folk traditions of her homeland. By founding the Little Carib Theatre in Port of Spain in 1947, she created the first permanent home for Caribbean folk dance, profoundly shaping the national identity of Trinidad and Tobago and influencing generations of artists across the West Indies. Her work elevated indigenous dance forms like the Bèlè, Limbo, and Shango from marginalized community practices to internationally celebrated art forms, fundamentally altering the cultural landscape of the region. ### Early Life and the Discovery of Folk Born on November 2, 1913, in the neighborhood of Woodbrook in Port of Spain, Trinidad, McBurnie was surrounded from an early age by the rhythmic and cultural diversity of the island. Trinidad was a melting pot of African, Indian, European, and Indigenous influences, but the formal education system and the colonial elite heavily favored Eurocentric culture. Despite this, the young Beryl was captivated by the songs, dances, and rituals of the ordinary people, which were often performed in the poorer neighborhoods. She recalled sneaking out of her middle-class home as a child to observe the Shango ceremonies, the stick-fighting yards, and the Carnival masquerades that took place in the working-class districts. These experiences left an indelible mark on her consciousness. Although she received formal training in classical piano and elocution at the Teachers' Training College, her true passion lay in movement. She recognized the inherent beauty, technical complexity, and historical significance of the folk dances that were routinely dismissed by the colonial authorities as "primitive" or "vulgar." > "Dance is the pulse of a nation. To deny our own rhythms is to deny our own soul." — Beryl McBurnie McBurnie began researching and documenting these traditional dances, traveling extensively across the island to learn the specific movements and rhythms of different rural communities. She understood that these dances were not merely entertainment; they were living repositories of history, survival, and resistance, passed down by enslaved ancestors and indentured laborers. ### The New York Years and "La Belle Rosette" In 1938, determined to broaden her horizons and formalize her training, McBurnie traveled to New York City. She enrolled at Columbia University, where she studied drama and movement. She also studied under modern dance pioneer Martha Graham, absorbing techniques that emphasized emotional expression and the dynamic use of the torso—elements that resonated deeply with African-derived dance forms. In New York, McBurnie immersed herself in the vibrant arts scene of the Harlem Renaissance and the emerging interest in Caribbean culture. She began performing under the stage name "La Belle Rosette" to immense acclaim. She introduced American audiences to Caribbean rhythms, performing at prestigious venues like the 92nd Street Y and the Village Vanguard. She also collaborated with prominent artists, including the legendary American singer, actor, and civil rights activist Paul Robeson. During this period, she popularized Calypso and Caribbean folk dance in the United States, bringing authentic Trinbagonian culture to an international audience. She even appeared in "soundies" (early musical short films), captivating audiences with her charismatic, dynamic, and unapologetically Caribbean performances. She was on the verge of major international stardom, but the pull of her homeland and her commitment to her people's culture proved stronger than the allure of Broadway. ### Return to Trinidad and The Little Carib Theatre In the early 1940s, McBurnie made the fateful decision to return to Trinidad. She abandoned a lucrative career in the US because she believed her true mission was to legitimize and elevate the folk arts in the Caribbean. Upon returning, she worked as a dance instructor for the Department of Education, boldly introducing folk dance into the school curriculum and challenging the absolute dominance of European ballet. ![Beryl McBurnie Video Thumbnail](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/WILLIE_WILLIE_1943_SOUNDIE_MUSIC_VIDEO_CALYPSO_MUSIC_SAM_MANNING_and_BELLE_ROSETTE.webm) Her most monumental achievement came in 1947 when she founded the Little Carib Theatre in the backyard of her family home on Roberts Street in Woodbrook. It was a modest, galvanized-roof structure, built largely through her sheer willpower and community support, but its cultural impact was revolutionary. The Little Carib became the first permanent theater and dance company in Trinidad dedicated to showcasing local arts. In 1948, the legendary Paul Robeson visited Trinidad specifically to lay the foundation stone for the Little Carib Theatre, a powerful testament to McBurnie's international stature and the political importance of her cultural project. The theater officially opened with a groundbreaking performance titled *Bele*, showcasing the traditional graceful dance of French and African origin, elevating it to high art. ### Championing Caribbean Culture and Identity The Little Carib Theatre became the epicenter of a cultural renaissance in the Caribbean. McBurnie rigorously trained a generation of dancers to perform the Bèlè, the Limbo (a feat of physical prowess originating from the cramped conditions of slave ships), the Kalinda (stick-fighting dance), and the Shango with dignity, precision, and theatrical flair. She proved to local audiences and international critics alike that these forms were as technically demanding and artistically valid as any European classical dance. Her work inspired artists across disciplines and provided a crucial cultural foundation as the nation moved toward independence. The Little Carib provided a safe and nurturing space for local musicians, playwrights, and painters. The renowned St. Lucian poet and Nobel Laureate [Derek Walcott](/profiles/derek-walcott) founded the Trinidad Theatre Workshop, which initially operated out of the Little Carib Theatre. Prominent cultural figures, including [Rex Nettleford](/profiles/rex-nettleford) of Jamaica, who later founded the National Dance Theatre Company of Jamaica, explicitly cited McBurnie as a primary inspiration for their own efforts to institutionalize Caribbean dance. Financial struggles were constant. McBurnie often funded the theater out of her own pocket, famously selling homemade pastelles and organizing tireless fundraisers to keep the doors open, driven by an unwavering belief in her mission. ### Legacy and Final Years Beryl McBurnie's contribution to the cultural landscape of the Caribbean cannot be overstated. She took the marginalized practices of the working class and elevated them to the national stage, forcing colonial society to recognize the beauty and validity of its own heritage. In doing so, she played a crucial role in the psychological decolonization of the Caribbean, instilling a sense of immense pride and self-worth in the people. She provided the essential cultural vocabulary that accompanied political independence in 1962. Her tireless efforts were recognized both locally and internationally. In 1959, she was made an Officer of the Order of the British Empire (OBE). In 1969, the Government of Trinidad and Tobago awarded her the Hummingbird Medal (Gold), and in 1989, she received the Trinity Cross, the nation's highest award, for her unparalleled service to the arts. McBurnie passed away on March 30, 2000, at the age of 86. Her legacy lives on not only in the continued existence of the Little Carib Theatre—which remains a vital cultural institution in Port of Spain—but in the very fabric of Trinidadian culture. Every time a folk dancer takes the stage, every time the rhythms of the Bèlè or the Shango echo through the Caribbean, the pioneering spirit of Beryl McBurnie dances with them.
